target_customer: Developers and companies that would pay per sample through an API for synthetic and cloned voices
problem: Text to speech sounded robotic and could not reproduce a specific person's voice without hours of recordings.
business_model: Usage-based API charging per voice sample requested, with first samples free (planned, per TechCrunch 2017)

founders.name: Alexandre de Brébisson
education: PhD student at the University of Montréal, MILA lab, advised by Yoshua Bengio (TechCrunch 2017)
founders.background_notes: Listed as founder and CEO on the YC page.

founders.name: Kundan Kumar
education: Researcher at the MILA lab, University of Montréal (YC page says the company grew out of MILA research)
founders.background_notes: YC bio says he led AI at Descript for five years after the acquisition and sits on Descript's board.

founders.name: Jose Sotelo
founders.background_notes: Listed as founder on the YC page.

competitors.name: Adobe Project VoCo
competitors.what: Voice editing prototype that needed roughly 20 minutes of source audio
competitors.traction_then: Demo only, not a shipped product

competitors.name: Google WaveNet
competitors.what: Neural network speech generation research rated closest to human speech

technical_complexity.rationale: Cloning a voice from about a minute of audio with deep learning in 2017 was research-grade, built on work from a university lab, though quality was still somewhat robotic.

defensibility.rationale: A research lead and talent gave an edge, but big labs published similar work and models could be reproduced; no data or network lock-in.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: Big labs kept publishing neural voice work, but none bought Lyrebird. Descript acquired it in September 2019 and turned the technology into its Overdub feature.

market_need_then: The April 2017 launch drew 100 thousand page visits and a million voice samples listened to in a day, showing curiosity, while coverage framed misuse and fake news risk; paying demand was not yet shown.

branding.name_origin: Named after the lyrebird, a bird that imitates the songs of other species and mechanical sounds (TechCrunch 2017).
branding.domain_note: Used lyrebird.ai; it now redirects to a Descript research page. Domain purchase history not found.

identity.voice_and_tone: Technical demo led, with ethics statements

branding.brand_signature: A demo conversation between synthetic Trump, Obama and Clinton voices

rebrands.why: Technology absorbed into Descript after the acquisition; the Lyrebird brand was retired.

branding.community_and_virality: The April 2017 demo spread widely in tech and general press, with coverage in TechCrunch, The Next Web and others; commenters also joked the name sounds like liar bird.

brand_strength.rationale: A vivid name that explains the product and a viral launch demo gave far more awareness than a 2017 startup of its size would usually get, though the brand ended with the acquisition.

outcome_analysis: Lyrebird came out of a university deep learning lab, launched with a viral voice cloning demo in April 2017 and drew heavy attention, but raised only the YC money before selling to Descript in September 2019 for undisclosed terms. The buyer wanted the technology for Overdub, and a founder stayed to lead AI there. It reads as a technical team and brand acquisition rather than a revenue story, with the public product shut down.
notes: The 120 thousand dollar YC amount and the 1.71 million PitchBook post money come from Voicebot (PitchBook estimate, so valuation_basis estimated); an aggregator also says a seed of 120 thousand. Village.ai claims Andreessen Horowitz, Redpoint and SVangel backing, which likely mixes up Descript's round and is not recorded. Acquisition terms undisclosed; whether the team joined Descript is not stated by Voicebot, though a founder's YC bio says he stayed. Founded year 2017 inferred from the YC batch and launch, not stated by a source. De Brebisson's and Kumar's education is stated only as MILA lab research (PhD student for de Brebisson). Competitors (VoCo, WaveNet) come from a Routenote summary of 2017 coverage; TechCrunch itself names none. Search results included some unrelated Lyrebird Health pages, ignored.
